strands.name: Ragusa · Dubrovnik
strands.intro: A refugee town on a rock became a merchant republic that kept its freedom for more than four centuries between Venice, Hungary and the Ottomans — under one word: LIBERTAS.

events.title: Founded by refugees from Epidaurum
events.text: Emperor Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio (c. 950) says people fleeing the Avar and Slav destruction of Epidaurum (Cavtat) settled the rock of Laus, the start of Ragusa. Digs under the cathedral have found older churches, so how old the settlement really is is still argued.

events.title: The Saracen siege
events.text: Arab raiders besieged the town for about fifteen months. It held until a Byzantine fleet of some 100 ships under Niketas Ooryphas came to its relief, and Byzantium then reorganised the coast as the Theme of Dalmatia.

events.title: St. Blaise becomes the city's patron
events.text: Tradition dates the Festivity of St. Blaise, held every 3 February, to 972; UNESCO's record traces it with certainty to 1190 and listed it as intangible heritage in 2009.
days: The Festivity of St. Blaise, Dubrovnik's patron

events.title: Lokrum's Benedictines
events.text: Benedictine monks are first recorded on Lokrum, the island off the city, in 1023. From 1859 it belonged to Archduke Maximilian of Austria, later Emperor of Mexico, who laid out its gardens.

events.title: Under Venice
events.text: After the Fourth Crusade Venice took sovereignty and chose the city’s count and archbishop, but Ragusa kept its own councils, laws and trade. Resentment boiled over in revolts in 1231, 1235 and 1251; Venetian rule ended in 1358.

events.title: Lastovo joins
events.text: The island of Lastovo placed itself under Ragusa of its own accord — by 1272 at the latest; the Dubrovnik diocese dates it to 1252.

events.title: The Statute of Dubrovnik
events.text: The city's law code, in eight books (the seventh is maritime law), framed Ragusan law until the Republic ended in 1808.
days: The Statute of Dubrovnik was promulgated

events.title: The notaries' books begin
events.text: The city hired a public notary, Tomasino de Savere. From here on contracts, wills and court business were written into registers that still survive in the State Archives in Dubrovnik — the oldest place to look for Ragusan families.

events.title: Ston and Pelješac bought
events.text: Ragusa bought Ston and the Pelješac peninsula from the Serbian king Stefan Dušan and the Bosnian ban Stjepan Kotromanić, then walled Ston to guard its salt pans.

events.title: Mljet
events.text: The island of Mljet came fully under Ragusa (the Great Council had first claimed it in 1301). The same year Mljet got its own statute, and its Benedictine abbey freed the islanders from their dues for a yearly 300 perpers.
src: Dubrovnik od XIII. do XV. stoljeća

events.title: Free of Venice
events.text: By the Treaty of Zadar Venice gave up Dalmatia. At Visegrád Ragusa accepted the Hungarian-Croatian king as distant overlord — and from then on governed itself as a republic.

events.title: The earliest known quarantine law
events.text: On 27 July 1377 the Great Council ordered that travellers from plague areas spend 30 days (the trentino) on the islet of Mrkan or in Cavtat before entering the city; the islets of Bobara and Supetar were used later too. The decree survives in the city’s law book, the Liber Viridis. The 40-day wait that later became the rule elsewhere, quaranta in Venetian, gave quarantine its name.
src: Quarantine, trade and health policies in Ragusa-Dubrovnik (PubMed)
days: Ragusa passed the earliest known quarantine law

events.title: The Littoral bought
events.text: King Ostoja of Bosnia sold Ragusa the coastland from Kuril to Ston, the Dubrovnik Littoral (Primorje), for 1,500 ducats, a house in the city and Ragusan citizenship. It was governed from Slano, whose first count took office in May 1399.

events.title: The slave trade banned
events.text: The council forbade citizens and foreigners alike to buy, sell or broker slaves in Ragusa or on its ships.
days: Ragusa banned the slave trade

events.title: Konavle bought
events.text: The Republic bought Konavle in two halves, the east in 1419 and the west in 1426 — the story is told in the Konavle strand. Its land now ran along the coast to Cape Oštro, at the mouth of the Bay of Kotor.

events.title: Water and bells
events.text: An aqueduct of about 12 km brought spring water from Šumet to Onofrio's fountains (1438–40); the bell tower on the Luža went up in 1444.

events.title: Tribute to the Sultan — and freedom kept
events.text: Ragusa began paying the Sultan a yearly tribute, the harač: 1,500 gold ducats, first handed over in Skopje in 1458, in return for its freedom and its merchants’ rights across Ottoman lands. The same year the Ragusan merchant Benedetto Cotrugli (Benedikt Kotruljević) wrote the earliest known description of double-entry bookkeeping; it was printed only in 1573.
src: Vesna Miović: Dubrovnik in Ottoman documents (Hrčak)
Turkish receipts for the Ragusan tribute (Hrčak)

events.title: The walls rise
events.text: With the Ottomans at the door after 1453, Minčeta became a great round tower and Revelin was built to guard the land gate.
src: Dubrovnik City Walls (Society of Friends of Dubrovnik Antiquities)

events.title: Dundo Maroje
events.text: Marin Držić’s comedy was first staged at Carnival in 1551, in the council hall beside the Rector’s Palace — the Golden Age of Ragusan letters.

events.title: The Great Earthquake
events.text: An earthquake and the fires after it all but razed the city; estimates of the dead run from about 3,000 to 5,000, the Rector among them. The cathedral and much of the Stradun were rebuilt afterwards, in the Baroque look you saw.
days: The Great Earthquake struck Dubrovnik

events.title: Buffers against Venice
events.text: At the peace of Karlowitz, after Ragusan diplomats lobbied in Vienna and Constantinople, the Ottomans kept two narrow outlets to the sea, at Neum–Klek and at Sutorina, so that Venetian land would not touch the Republic’s — which is why Bosnia and Herzegovina still reaches the sea at Neum.

events.title: Ruđer Bošković born
events.text: The Ragusan Jesuit became one of Europe's great scientists — physicist, astronomer and founder of the Brera observatory in Milan. Dubrovnik's airport is named for him.
days: Ruđer Bošković was born in Dubrovnik

events.title: The French arrive
events.text: On 27 May 1806 French troops under General Lauriston entered the city. From 17 June Russian and Montenegrin forces besieged it, burning the suburbs and the summer villas, until a French relief force under General Molitor drove them off on 6 July.
src: Matica hrvatska: the war round Dubrovnik in 1806
days: French troops entered Dubrovnik

events.title: The Republic ends
events.text: Marshal Marmont abolished the Republic of Ragusa. After Napoleon's fall the Congress of Vienna (1815) gave it to Austria, and it was never restored.
days: Marmont abolished the Republic of Ragusa

events.title: The Partisans enter
events.text: German troops left and Yugoslav Partisans took the city on 18 October 1944. They arrested more than 300 citizens, and on 24–25 October executed 53 men without trial on the island of Daksa (some sources say 48); the remains of 53 were found there in 2009.
days: Yugoslav Partisans entered Dubrovnik

events.title: World Heritage
events.text: The Old City was added to UNESCO's World Heritage List.

events.title: The siege
events.text: The Yugoslav navy blockaded the city’s waters from 17 September 1991, and the army besieged Dubrovnik from 1 October 1991 until its defenders broke out on 26 May 1992. The worst attack came on 6 December 1991; Fort Imperial on Srđ held.
src: Museum of the Homeland War Dubrovnik
Hrvatski vojnik: the lifting of the siege

events.title: The Pelješac Bridge
events.text: The bridge joined the Dubrovnik area to the rest of Croatia by road without crossing Neum.
days: The Pelješac Bridge opened

strands.name: Konavle
strands.intro: The fertile valley south of Dubrovnik — older than the city itself, fought over by Serbian, Bosnian and Herzegovinian lords, then Ragusan farmland for almost 400 years.

events.title: Epidauros
events.text: Cavtat began as Epidauros, a settlement on the Illyrian coast. Some accounts call it a Greek colony; Croatian archaeologists note there isn't enough evidence to say so.

events.title: Roman Epidaurum
events.text: Epidaurum was made a Roman colony, by most accounts in Caesar's time, as a reward for backing the winning side in Rome's civil war. Traces of its field grid, villas, an aqueduct near Vodovađa and a Mithras relief at Močići survive in Konavle.

events.title: A bishop of Epidaurum
events.text: Epidaurum had become a bishop's seat; its bishop took part in the Church councils held at Salona in the 530s.

events.title: Destroyed — and reborn as Ragusa
events.text: Avars and Slavs destroyed Epidaurum; by tradition its people fled to found Ragusa. The town that grew again on the site was long called Ragusa Vecchia, 'Old Ragusa'.

events.title: Konavli in Travunia
events.text: Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio has a chapter "Of the Terbounians and Kanalites": the Kanalites were the Slavs of Konavle, ruled together with Travunia between Ragusa and the Bay of Kotor.

events.title: Under the Nemanjić
events.text: Stefan Nemanja brought Travunia, and with it Konavle, under Serbian rule. It stayed Serbian until the Nemanjić line ended in 1371, then passed through the hands of local lords.

events.title: Lords come and go
events.text: After the Serbian empire broke up, Konavle passed to Nikola Altomanović, then the Balšić lords of Zeta. In 1377–78 King Tvrtko I took it for Bosnia, and the Sanković family held it for him. Sokol Grad, the fortress above Dunave, first appears in records in 1373.

events.title: A sale blocked
events.text: On 15 April 1391 the Sanković brothers sold Konavle to Ragusa, without the Bosnian king’s consent. Before Ragusa could take it, the Bosnian lords Vlatko Vuković and Pavle Radinović seized Radič Sanković and split Konavle between themselves.
src: Paula Kaulić: Ragusa’s expansion into Konavle (Hrčak)

events.title: Upper Konavle bought
events.text: Sandalj Hranić sold the eastern half to Ragusa for 12,000 ducats and a yearly 500 perpers.

events.title: Lower Konavle and Cavtat bought
events.text: Radoslav Pavlović sold the western half, with Cavtat and Obod, for 18,000 perpers (the deed is dated 31 December 1426). From 1427 a Ragusan rector governed Konavle from his palace at Pridvorje until 1808.
days: Ragusa bought Lower Konavle and Cavtat
events.places: ^(?!Ludo More)(.*(Luka Cavtat|Žal|Tiha Bay \(Uvala Tiha\)|Old City \(Stari grad\)), Cavtat$|.*Cavtat Harbor)

events.title: The Konavle War
events.text: Radoslav Pavlović tried to take back what he had sold. The war ended in 1432 with Konavle staying Ragusan.

events.title: Herceg Stjepan's war
events.text: Stjepan Vukčić Kosača, Sandalj’s nephew, went to war with Ragusa over trade and over Konavle, and his troops overran it. Peace came on 10 April 1454 with nothing settled, and Konavle stayed Ragusan.

events.title: Sokol Grad on guard
events.text: Sokol Grad, the fortress above Dunave, came to the Republic with Konavle and was kept with a garrison under a Ragusan castellan. It no longer appears as a military post in the records of 1672, and was probably abandoned around then.
src: Total Croatia: the Republic’s highest fortress

events.title: The Konavle Revolt
events.text: Rising dues, labour on noble estates and a 10 May 1799 order forcing everyone over 15 to buy state salt drove more than 800 Konavle householders to resist ("Nećete pro Zvekovice"). The revolt failed, but showed how weak the Republic had become.
days: The salt order that sparked the Konavle Revolt

events.title: War reaches Cavtat
events.text: Russian and Montenegrin forces crossed into Konavle. On 30 May about a hundred French soldiers held off some 300 Montenegrins near Zvekovica for hours, but on 3 June the French left Cavtat, and its people went with them. Cavtat was looted, and around 235 houses in Konavle — about a quarter of them — were burned.
days: French troops held off Montenegrin forces near Zvekovica
The French left Cavtat

events.title: Two sons of Cavtat
events.text: The jurist Baltazar Bogišić (1834–1908) and the painter Vlaho Bukovac (1855–1922) were both born in Cavtat; Bukovac's birth house is now a museum.

events.title: From Gruda to Čilipi
events.text: Flights began at an airfield at Gruda in 1936; the present airport at Čilipi opened in 1962.

events.title: Konavle cut in two
events.text: In 1941 western Konavle, run from Cavtat, went to the Axis Independent State of Croatia; the east around Gruda was annexed by Italy, which took Kuna and Pridvorje too in 1942. When Italy surrendered, German troops entered Cavtat on 9 September 1943.
src: Konavle u Drugom svjetskom ratu (Konavle museums)
days: German troops entered Cavtat

events.title: Occupied
events.text: The first shells fell on 22 September 1991, on Đurinići and Vitaljina in eastern Konavle. Yugoslav army units burned Čilipi between 5 and 7 October 1991 (an indictment lists 90 family houses destroyed) and took Cavtat on 15 October. Konavle stayed occupied for a year, and many of its people were held at Morinj in Montenegro; its villages were rebuilt over the years that followed.

events.title: Freed
events.text: Under the Tuđman–Ćosić agreement of 30 September 1992 the Yugoslav army withdrew, and Operation Konavle, from the night of 20–21 October 1992, freed the last occupied part of the Dubrovnik area.

events.title: Epidaurum still giving up secrets
events.text: Konavle's museum archaeologists found a sealed, untouched late Roman stone sarcophagus (4th–6th century) in Epidaurum's cemetery in Cavtat.

strands.name: Dalmatia
strands.intro: The long coast Ragusa belonged to and stood apart from: Illyrian, Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Croatian, Hungarian, Venetian, Austrian — and Croatian again.

events.title: Illyrians and Greeks
events.text: The coast is Illyrian land (the Delmatae tribe gave Dalmatia its name), with Greek colonies on the islands: Issa on Vis, founded by Dionysius of Syracuse in the 390s BC, and Pharos on Hvar, from about 385 BC.
src: Hrvatska enciklopedija: Greek colonisation of the Adriatic

events.title: Rome arrives
events.text: Rome fought the Illyrian queen Teuta and began two centuries of conquest. It took Salona in 78 BC.

events.title: The Great Illyrian Revolt
events.text: After crushing the revolt Rome organised the province of Dalmatia, with its capital at Salona near Split.

events.title: Diocletian's palace
events.text: The Dalmatian-born emperor built his retirement palace at Spalatum — the heart of today's Split.

events.title: The last Western emperor
events.text: Julius Nepos, driven out of Italy in 475, went on ruling from Dalmatia, still recognised in Constantinople as Western emperor, until he was murdered in Diocletian’s palace on 9 May 480. The Ostrogoths took the province in 493; Justinian’s armies won it back from 535.

events.title: Salona falls, Split is born
events.text: Avar and Slav invasions ended Roman Salona; its people moved into Diocletian's palace. Byzantium kept only the islands and a few coast towns — Zadar, Split, Trogir and Ragusa among them.

events.title: The Theme of Dalmatia
events.text: Byzantium governed its Dalmatian towns as a province ruled from Zadar, until about 1060.

events.title: Kings of Croatia and Dalmatia
events.text: Pope John X’s letter of 925 calls Tomislav king of the Croats. Peter Krešimir IV is the first ruler recorded as king of Croatia and Dalmatia, and from about 1069 the Dalmatian towns came under his crown.

events.title: Union with Hungary
events.text: Croatia and Dalmatia came under the Hungarian king. The famous Pacta conventa describing the deal is now thought to be a later copy or forgery.

events.title: Venice out
events.text: The Treaty of Zadar made Venice give up Dalmatia to Louis I of Hungary — the same deal that freed Ragusa.

events.title: Sold to Venice
events.text: Ladislaus of Naples sold his claim to Dalmatia to Venice for 100,000 ducats; by 1420 Venice ruled the coast, which it kept until 1797. Ragusa stayed outside.
days: Ladislaus of Naples sold his claim to Dalmatia to Venice

events.title: Venice falls
events.text: Austria took Venetian Dalmatia in 1797; Napoleon's France had it from 1805/06 and folded it, with Ragusa, into the Illyrian Provinces; the Congress of Vienna returned it all to Austria.

events.title: The Kingdom of Dalmatia
events.text: An Austrian crown land, then part of Austria-Hungary, with its capital at Zadar — Dubrovnik and Konavle included.

events.title: Into Yugoslavia
events.text: Dalmatia joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (Yugoslavia from 1929). Under the Treaty of Rapallo (1920) Zadar and the island of Lastovo went to Italy, which kept them until 1947.

events.title: Divided by the Axis
events.text: The Treaties of Rome (18 May 1941) gave Italy much of the coast as the Governorate of Dalmatia — near Dubrovnik, the islands of Korčula and Mljet — while Šipan, Lopud and Lokrum stayed in the Independent State of Croatia. Italy's surrender in September 1943 ended the arrangement.
days: The Treaties of Rome divided Dalmatia

events.title: Croatia
events.text: Dalmatia became part of independent Croatia, at the price of the Homeland War of 1991–95.

strands.name: The siege · 1991–92
strands.intro: From October 1991 to May 1992 Dubrovnik was cut off by land and sea and shelled by the Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA), the Montenegrin Territorial Defence and volunteers from Montenegro and eastern Herzegovina. Its defenders, few and poorly armed at first, never let the city fall. Here is the siege in dates, and the places on your trip where it happened.

events.title: The blockade
events.text: On 17 September 1991 the Yugoslav navy began a full blockade of Dubrovnik’s waters. For months, ships bound for the city were stopped and searched.
src: HU Benedikt: the naval blockade of Croatia
days: The Yugoslav navy began its blockade of Dubrovnik’s waters

events.title: The commander
events.text: Nojko Marinović, a JNA officer commanding the barracks at Trebinje, crossed to the Croatian side on 19 September 1991, bringing the army’s plans for the attack on Dubrovnik. He led the city’s defence with a few hundred poorly armed police, Croatian National Guard and local volunteers. He was badly wounded by a landmine in March 1992, and died in 2021.
days: Nojko Marinović, who would lead the defence of Dubrovnik, crossed to the Croatian side

events.title: The first shells
events.text: The war reached the Dubrovnik area on 22 September 1991, when mortar fire hit Đurinići and Vitaljina in eastern Konavle. The next day artillery struck Vitaljina and Brgat, and the first villagers were evacuated.
days: The first shells fell on Đurinići and Vitaljina in Konavle

events.title: The Armed Boats Squadron
events.text: Local volunteers with fast boats formed the Armed Boats Squadron (Odred naoružanih brodova). Its first boat, the Sveti Vlaho, sailed on 23 September 1991, and through the siege its crews ran the blockade to keep a supply line open by sea.
days: The Armed Boats Squadron’s first boat sailed to run the blockade

events.title: The attack begins
events.text: At dawn on 1 October 1991 the JNA, the Montenegrin Territorial Defence and volunteers from Montenegro and eastern Herzegovina attacked from land, sea and air. Jets hit the transmitter on Srđ, and the city lost electricity and water when the Komolac substation was destroyed. The attackers expected Dubrovnik to fall within days.
src: Morski.hr: the plan for Dubrovnik to fall in five days
days: The attack on Dubrovnik began

events.title: Morinj
events.text: From 3 October 1991 the JNA held prisoners from the Dubrovnik area, most of them from Konavle, in a camp at Morinj on the Bay of Kotor in Montenegro. Around 300 people passed through it before it closed in 1992; former prisoners told of constant beatings. A Montenegrin court later convicted four former reservists.

events.title: Slano and Čilipi
events.text: Slano, in the Dubrovnik Littoral, fell on 4–5 October 1991. Between 5 and 7 October army units burned Čilipi (an indictment lists 90 family houses destroyed), and the airport you flew into was looted, its equipment partly carried off to Montenegro.
src: Vreme: equipment taken from the airport

events.title: Cavtat falls
events.text: The army took Cavtat on 15 October 1991, and Župa dubrovačka in the days after 22 October. By the end of November it held almost all the land between Pelješac and Prevlaka except Dubrovnik itself.
src: Domovinski rat: the occupation of Župa

events.title: The Libertas convoy
events.text: Led by the ferry Slavija, which had left Rijeka on 28 October, a convoy of civilian boats sailed through the blockade with aid, with Stjepan Mesić, then President of the Yugoslav Presidency, aboard. It reached Dubrovnik on 31 October. On 14 November the Slavija left the port of Gruž for Rijeka with almost 4,000 people, most of them elderly people, women and children.
src: Domovinski rat: the Libertas convoy reaches Dubrovnik
days: The Libertas convoy reached Dubrovnik through the blockade
The ferry Slavija carried almost 4,000 people out of Gruž

events.title: The ring closes
events.text: Bosanka, on the plateau behind Srđ, fell on 9 November 1991 after hard fighting in which several defenders were killed. In late November, after Osojnik, Mokošica and the villages of Rijeka dubrovačka were occupied. Shells fell on Gruž, Lapad and Babin Kuk, including hotels full of refugees.
src: Identitet: the defence of Dubrovnik, part II
days: Bosanka, on the plateau behind Srđ, fell after hard fighting

events.title: A city of refugees
events.text: Thousands of people driven from Konavle, Župa and the Littoral were sheltered in Dubrovnik’s hotels, from Lapad and Babin Kuk, where you stayed, to the Imperial by the Pile Gate, whose top floor burned in the shelling. The city lived without mains electricity or water.
src: Identitet: the defence of Dubrovnik, part II

events.title: The darkest day
events.text: From before dawn the army shelled the city for more than ten hours, and attacked Srđ with infantry and tanks from Bosanka and Strinčjera. A few dozen defenders held Fort Imperial, with tanks right up at the fort; had it fallen, the city lay open below. In the Old Town fires gutted palaces, among them the one on Od Sigurate that housed the Dubrovnik Summer Festival, and the UN tribunal later found that the attack answered no Croatian military position. Nineteen people, civilians and defenders, were killed that day and about sixty wounded. Among the dead was the photographer Pavo Urban, 23, killed while photographing the shelling; a plaque under the city bell tower marks where he fell. 6 December is Dubrovnik Defenders’ Day.
src: The role of Fort Imperial in the defence of Dubrovnik (ResearchGate)
Museum of the Homeland War Dubrovnik: 6 December
days: The worst attack on Dubrovnik; Fort Imperial held. Dubrovnik Defenders’ Day

events.title: World Heritage in Danger
events.text: Meeting in Carthage in December 1991, after UNESCO’s observers reported on the attack of 6 December, the World Heritage Committee put the Old City on its List of World Heritage in Danger.
src: City of Dubrovnik: the role of UNESCO observers

events.title: The siege broken
events.text: As the JNA began to pull back, Dubrovnik’s defenders, by now the 163rd Brigade, broke out of the city on 26 May 1992, freeing Rijeka dubrovačka, Župa, Brgat, Orašac and Osojnik, and joined the 1st Guards Brigade fighting its way down the coast from the west. The shelling did not stop at once: the city was hit again on 29 May. By the end of June the Dubrovnik Littoral was free.
src: Hrvatski vojnik: the liberation of the south and the lifting of the siege
Museum of the Homeland War Dubrovnik
days: Dubrovnik’s defenders broke the siege

events.title: Konavle freed
events.text: Under the Tuđman–Ćosić agreement, signed in Geneva on 30 September 1992, the Yugoslav army left Konavle; its last soldiers left Prevlaka on the evening of 20 October. That night Operation Konavle began with a landing at Cavtat, and by 24 October Croatian forces stood on the borders. Prevlaka was placed under UN supervision.
days: Operation Konavle: the last occupied part of the Dubrovnik area was freed

events.title: The damage and the repair
events.text: About 2,000 shells and rockets struck the Old Town: 594 of its 824 buildings were damaged and the walls took more than a hundred direct hits. Restoration followed, and in 1998 UNESCO took the Old City off its In Danger list. A map of the hits stands near the Pile Gate.
src: City of Dubrovnik: destruction in the Old City
UNESCO: Dubrovnik removed from the Danger List
HMdb: the map of the damage

events.title: Judgement at The Hague
events.text: At the UN tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Admiral Miodrag Jokić pleaded guilty over the attack of 6 December and was sentenced to seven years in 2004. General Pavle Strugar was convicted in 2005 for failing to stop it and sentenced to eight years, reduced on appeal in 2008 to seven and a half.

events.title: Remembering
events.text: Croatian accounts count 182 defenders from Dubrovnik’s own units, and some 235 from other Croatian units, killed in the defence and liberation of the Dubrovnik area, and between 82 and 92 civilians. The photographs of Dubrovnik’s fallen defenders hang in the Memorial Room in the Sponza Palace; Fort Imperial houses the Museum of the Homeland War. The cross on Srđ, pulled down in 1991, was raised again in October 1997, and the cable car, wrecked in 1991, has run again since July 2010.
src: Museum of the Homeland War Dubrovnik
events.places: ^Dubrovnik Cable Car|^Mount Srđ Cross|^Observation Deck, Mount Srđ

records.title: Finding the family in the records
points: Church birth (baptism) registers only became compulsory with the Council of Trent’s decree of 11 November 1563. Croatia’s oldest parish register is Umag’s in Istria, from 1483, though its earliest entries survive as copies made after 1608; in the Dubrovnik area the oldest is a 1580 death register from Suđurađ on Šipan.

For the 1400s, Ragusa's own government records are where families appear: the notarial and chancery books (Diversa Notariae, Diversa Cancellariae) and registered wills (Testamenta Notariae), kept from 1278–1282 onward in the State Archives in Dubrovnik, plus confraternity rolls such as the Antunini register.

Konavle became Ragusan in 1419–1426, so from then on Konavle families turn up in the Republic's land, tax and court records. Konavle's surviving parish registers mostly begin in the late 1700s (Veljaci's baptisms run from 1786).
Parish registers taken after 1945 were returned to the Dubrovnik diocese in 2022; FamilySearch also holds digitised Croatian church books.
src: Umag baptismal register 1483–1643 (State Archives in Pazin)
